items.title: No randomised evidence in this network
items.whyItMatters: A before-and-after switch would be confounded by next year's order set change.
items.opportunity: Randomise wards to tiered or standard display for six months.

items.title: Override rate is a poor primary outcome
items.whyItMatters: Most overrides are appropriate (claim c4), so a falling override rate need not mean better care.
items.opportunity: Use appropriate response to high-severity alerts, judged on a random sample by pharmacists.

items.title: Harm from suppressed moderate interactions
items.whyItMatters: Tiering moves moderate interactions to a passive note (claim c3).
items.opportunity: Targeted surveillance of high-risk moderate combinations in both arms.

items.title: Contamination by rotating prescribers
items.whyItMatters: Prescriber randomisation would expose many orders to the other arm (claim c2).
items.opportunity: Randomise wards, stratify by hospital and specialty, and record prescriber rotation.

items.title: Older adults with kidney impairment carry the risk
items.whyItMatters: Potassium-raising combinations dominated harm after tiering.
items.opportunity: Keep potassium-raising combinations interruptive for patients with reduced kidney function in both arms.

errorsFound: The request treats override rates as the measure of alert fatigue; the appraised evidence shows most overrides are appropriate.
reevaluation: The gaps confirm a ward-randomised trial with an appropriateness outcome and a harm safeguard.
summary: Five gaps; the absent randomised evidence and the outcome definition are high severity.
